newsitem.title: USA: INSIGHT--Little relief seen from COMEX gold slump.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT--Little relief seen from COMEX gold slump.

text.p: COMEX gold futures remain in their three-week downtrend, with little sign of an imminent bounce after falling to two-month lows Friday, though technical indicators look oversold, analysts said.

"Precious metals remain lackluster, with fund selling continuing to weigh on the complex, and its hard to see what's going to provide the fundamentals for a bounce," ABN Amro Bank's New York-based vice president Ron Spurga said.
"Auto industry demand (for platinum group metals) is soft, we got no bounce on the tensions in Iraq earlier this month, and we may not even get a bounce if (Russian President) Yeltsin dies," he said.
COMEX December gold was down 10 cents at $383.80 an ounce midsession Monday, after falling to a three-year intraday low for the December contract Friday at $383.30.

On the daily charts for December gold, the popular four, nine and 18-day triple moving-average trend-following indicator remains in its downtrend since early September, with the four-day average below the nine-day average and the nine-day average below the 18-day average.
But the standard nine-day relative strength indicator (RSI) is in the oversold zone below 20 percent, closing at 18 percent Friday, suggesting a bounce was possible, analysts said.
In New York bullion trade, spot gold was quoted $381.10/381/60 midsession Monday, from a London afternoon fix Monday at $381.00, and a New York close Friday at $380.85/381/35.

"Traders still seem intent on pushing (spot) gold prices through support at the $380 level and should this level give way, the next stop is $374," CPM Group analyst Edward Kempf said. "On the other hand should $380 hold fast, prices would be expected to reverse direction and test resistance at $386."
Both gold and silver are now near the bottom of ranges that have provided value in the past two or three years, analysts noted.
In the bullion market, spot silver fell to 18-month lows Friday, while spot gold and platinum saw fresh two-month lows, and palladium saw a fresh three-year low Monday morning.

"The specter of potential IMF gold sales has been weighing on gold," Merrill Lynch analyst Ted Arnold said in a weekly report. "While we think the long term implications of the sale of five million ounces of IMF gold are not great, the short term psychological impact has resulted in a series of knee-jerk reactions."

The IMF last week failed to reach agreement on the plan to sell some of its 104 million ounce gold reserve to finance its developing country debt relief plan, but the issue may be discussed again by the IMF interim-policy making committee on September 29.

"Not all the news is bearish, though, with recent Russian data indicating Russia's gold production plunged 18.68 percent in the first eight months of 1996, mainly as a result of the government's inability to pay bills," Arnold said.
According to Interfax News, Rusia produced 64.368 tonnes of gold in the first eight months of 1996, down 10.133 tonnes from the same period last year, Arnold noted.
"The recent decline in gold prices also reflects expectations that the U.S. Federal Reserve will tighten monetary policy at its September 24 FOMC meeting," Smith Barney analyst David Rinehimer said.

"The gold market has reacted negatively to the potential for monetary tightening, since rising interest rates increase the cost of holding gold, dampen inflationary expectations and enhance the yield of competing paper assets," he said.
--Clive McKeef, New York Commodities Desk, +1-212-859-1641; email: clive.mckeef@reuters.com
